title: Diagnosing Skin Disease and Mildew
summary: The LORD gives Moses and Aaron detailed instructions for how a priest is to examine swellings, rashes, spots, boils, burns, scalp infections, and baldness, deciding whether a person is clean or unclean, often after one or two seven-day periods of isolation. A person declared unclean must tear his clothes, cover his mouth, call out a warning, and live outside the camp. The chapter closes with the same process applied to mildew in fabric and leather.
story: Leviticus 11 to 15 is a block of laws about clean and unclean: animals for food (chapter 11), childbirth (chapter 12), and now the skin. These laws exist because of what happened at the end of Exodus, when the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle and God came to live in the middle of Israel's camp. A holy God dwelling among a people who get sick, give birth, and die raises a practical question: how does the camp stay fit for his presence? Chapter 13 answers for one of the most visible threats, the skin disease the Hebrew calls tsara'at. Chapter 14 will describe how a person who recovers is brought back in, and chapter 15 turns to bodily discharges. All of it prepares for the Day of Atonement in chapter 16, where the whole camp's uncleanness is dealt with at once.
historical:
The setting given by the book is the wilderness of Sinai, in the year after Israel left Egypt, with the tabernacle newly set up. When Leviticus reached its final form is debated in the same way as the rest of the Pentateuch: tradition credits Moses, while many critical scholars assign these laws to a priestly source edited in or after the Babylonian exile, and others argue the priestly material preserves much older practice. On any view, these are the procedures of Israel's priesthood, the men descended from Aaron who served at the sanctuary.

The disease itself is hard to identify. Older English Bibles translated tsara'at as leprosy, because the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint, made in Egypt in the last centuries BC) used the Greek word lepra, a term Greek writers used for scaly skin conditions. Modern leprosy, Hansen's disease, is named for the Norwegian physician who identified its bacterium in 1873, and its classic marks (numbness, loss of sensation, deformity of hands and feet) are not what this chapter describes. The symptoms here, white patches, scaling, raw flesh, and spreading, fit a range of conditions, and the same word covers mold in cloth (verses 47 to 59) and in houses (chapter 14). That is why the BSB uses phrases like skin disease and mildew. The category is ritual and visible rather than a single medical diagnosis.
cultural:
The priest here is not a physician. He prescribes no treatment and offers no cure; his job is to look and to pronounce. The phrase “the priest must pronounce him unclean” and its opposite run through the chapter like a refrain, because a priestly declaration settled a person's status in the community. Being unclean was not the same as being sinful. Many ordinary and even good things, like childbirth or burying a parent, made a person unclean for a time. Uncleanness meant a person could not approach the sanctuary or touch holy things until the condition passed and the proper steps were taken.

The instructions in verses 45 and 46 carried heavy social weight. Torn clothes and loose, unkempt hair were the signs of mourning in Israel, the way people looked at a funeral. A person with tsara'at looked like a mourner, and in a sense was one, cut off from ordinary life. Covering the mouth (literally the upper lip or mustache) and calling out a warning kept others from accidental contact. The sentence “He must live alone in a place outside the camp” meant separation from family, worship, and daily work for as long as the disease lasted. At the same time, the repeated seven-day waiting periods protected people from being expelled on a first glance, and the surprising rule of verses 12 and 13 (a person covered entirely in white is clean) shows that the concern was raw, open, changing flesh rather than simply looking unwell.
literary: This is case law written as a priestly manual. Each paragraph opens with a condition (“When someone has”, “When a boil appears”, “When there is a burn”, “If a man or woman has an infection on the head or chin”), then lists what the priest should look for: whether the hair has turned white, yellow, or black, whether the spot appears deeper than the skin, whether it has spread. The verbs examine, isolate, reexamine, and pronounce repeat in a fixed order, which made the procedure easy to learn and hard to bend. The chapter moves from the body to the garment, and verse 59 closes with a summary formula, “This is the law concerning”, of the kind that frames many sections of Leviticus.

outline.t: Swellings, rashes, and bright spots: examination and isolation
Scaly outbreaks on the head or chin
Harmless spots, baldness, and sores on the scalp
The life of a person declared unclean
Mildew in wool, linen, and leather

doctrines.note: God's holy presence in the camp shapes how Israel treats even the surface of the body. The line between clean and unclean taught Israel every day that approaching God is not casual and that life in his presence is meant to be whole.

The law here is careful and patient: repeated examinations, waiting periods, and clear criteria guard both the community and the individual from a hasty judgment. The torah (instruction) of verse 59 is practical wisdom for ordinary life, not only rules for worship.

The chapter does not explain why anyone gets sick or say the sick person has sinned. It does show how heavy illness could be when it also meant isolation, a burden later answered by Jesus's willingness to touch the unclean.

words.note: Tsara'at, traditionally translated leprosy. It names a visible, spreading surface condition on skin, fabric, leather, or plaster, not one specific disease. Its key features in this chapter are appearance and change, which is why the priest looks and waits rather than treats.

Nega, a blow, stroke, or plague, and here an infection or mark. The word comes from the verb to touch or strike and appears 47 times in this chapter. Elsewhere it can describe a blow from God (the plagues on Egypt use the same root), though this chapter itself makes no such claim about the cases it describes.

Tame, unclean. In Leviticus it describes a ritual status, not dirt and not necessarily guilt. An unclean person was barred from holy things until cleansed. The same root supplies the verb the priest uses when he pronounces someone unclean.

Taher, to be clean or pure, the opposite status. The priest's declaration of clean restored a person to the full life of the community and the worship of Israel, and the washing of clothes marked the change.

christ: The Gospels deliberately recall this chapter. A man with a skin disease comes to Jesus asking to be made clean, and Jesus touches him before he heals him, then sends him to show himself to the priest as the law of Moses required (Mark 1:40-44; Matthew 8:2-4; Luke 5:12-14). Under this chapter's logic, touching such a man should have made Jesus unclean; instead the cleanness flowed the other way. Luke also tells of ten men with the disease who stand at a distance and call out to Jesus, exactly as verses 45 and 46 required, and are cleansed on their way to the priests (Luke 17:11-19). The Letter to the Hebrews says Jesus suffered outside the city gate and calls his followers to go to him outside the camp (Hebrews 13:12-13), using the language of the place where the unclean lived. The link between this chapter and Christ is not a prediction; it is a pattern the New Testament writers saw, in which the one who is holy goes to the place of exclusion to bring people home.

hard.q: Why would God require sick people to be pushed out of the community?
hard.a:
The command in verse 46 is hard to read, and it was hard to live. Interpreters answer in several ways. Some stress public health: isolation, waiting periods, and burning contaminated cloth would have limited the spread of some infections, whatever the ancient understanding of disease. Others, including Jacob Milgrom in his large commentary on Leviticus and Gordon Wenham in his, argue that the logic is mainly symbolic: flaking, decaying skin looked like death, and the laws kept the signs of death away from the sanctuary of the living God, teaching that he is the God of life and wholeness. The anthropologist Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), influentially read such rules as a way of ordering the world into clear categories.

What the chapter does not say also matters. It never calls the sick person a sinner, and it builds in patience and a way back (chapter 14 is the ceremony of return). Separation was tied to the condition, not the person, and it lasted only as long as the disease. Israel's later history shows the exclusion could harden into contempt, which is part of why Jesus's touch of an unclean man was so startling.

questions: The priest had to look carefully and wait before pronouncing anyone unclean. Where are you quick to label people, and what would patient looking change?
Who lives outside the camp in your community, cut off by illness, reputation, or circumstance, and what would it mean to go to them?
Uncleanness in Leviticus was a condition, not always a sin. How does that distinction change the way you think about your own weakness or someone else's?
